Detect and classify intersections between distinct contours

Source: R/geometry.R
detect_junctions.Rd

Returns T, Y, X, Arrow and Star junctions. Same-contour self crossings and collinear overlaps have no unique intersection and are excluded. Proximate intersections merge by connected components, including transitive chains.

Usage

detect_junctions(
  x,
  absolute_epsilon = 1,
  relative_epsilon = 0.3,
  merge_radius = 2,
  endpoint_radius = 2,
  method = c("sweep", "exhaustive"),
  gap_metric = c("euclidean", "chebyshev"),
  rule = c("exit", "mlv2023")
)

Arguments

x

A drawing.

absolute_epsilon

Maximum endpoint extension in pixels, measured according to `gap_metric`.

relative_epsilon

Maximum endpoint extension as a segment fraction; the stricter of the two limits applies.

merge_radius

Radius for merging nearby intersections.

endpoint_radius

Radius of the junction neighbourhood that arms must leave.

method

Exact sweep candidate filtering or exhaustive pair enumeration.

gap_metric

How `absolute_epsilon` is measured along a segment. `"euclidean"` (default) measures length and is rotation invariant. `"chebyshev"` (as in MLV) counts the larger coordinate change, so an extension reaches one raster step: up to `sqrt(2)` pixels along a diagonal.

rule

Junction definition. `"exit"` (default) is the definition described in Details. `"mlv2023"` reproduces the MLV MATLAB toolbox (commit f12418a), including each recorded difference (MLV-M006 to M008, M019, M021 to M026 in DIFFERENCES.md): endpoint snapping, discarded negative coordinates, order-dependent merging, start-first arm attachment and adjacent-segment arms, no wrapping of closed contours, and its interior-arm angle convention. It always uses the Chebyshev gap and the exhaustive pair order; `method` is ignored and `gap_metric` may only be `"chebyshev"`. Its members list the adjacent segments MLV adds. Use it only to reproduce published MLV values.

Value

A data frame with one row per junction: `junction_id`, position `x`, `y`, `type`, `min_angle` and `max_angle` (degrees), and three list columns:

`arms`

The orientation of each arm, in degrees from 0 to 360, counterclockwise from the positive x axis in the drawing convention (image y pointing down, so 90 points up the screen), sorted increasing. Two arms can share an orientation.

`angles`

The gaps between consecutive arms. With `n` arms, `angles[k] = arms[k + 1] - arms[k]` for `k < n`, and the last gap wraps around: `angles[n] = arms[1] + 360 - arms[n]`. Under the default rule the gaps sum to 360.

`members`

The incident contour and segment indices.

Under `rule = "mlv2023"`, `arms` are the directions MLV itself assigns, not directions in the drawing convention. A segment that starts or ends within `endpoint_radius` of the junction position contributes its orientation pointing away from that end, and its neighbouring segment in the contour contributes one more arm (MLV-M024). A segment that passes the junction contributes, for each of its two ends, the direction from that end towards the junction position computed with y pointing up (MLV-M007). On diagonal segments these arms are therefore mirrored, and they can coincide with other arms. `angles` are computed from these arms exactly as above, modulo 360.

Details

For the default `rule = "exit"`, arms are defined on the junction neighbourhood: the union of open discs of radius `endpoint_radius` around every intersection merged into the junction, so each merged crossing keeps its arms. Each incident contour contributes one arm for each direction in which it leaves that region, following the contour past vertices inside it; a contour that ends inside the region contributes no arm in that direction. A segment that never enters the region and lies wholly beyond its intersections (a gap wider than the radius) contributes only its arm leaving away from them. Closed contours wrap around. Overshoots, gaps and contour pieces shorter than the radius are therefore part of the junction, and the result does not depend on contour direction, numbering or start vertex. An arm's direction is the orientation of the segment through which it leaves, pointing away from the junction, so angles between straight arms do not depend on the merged position. Junctions with fewer than three arms are dropped. An endpoint extension exactly equal to its limit is accepted. Angles use the drawing convention: counterclockwise degrees, image y down.
